method_card.title: Tally Charts, Tabulation and Pictograms
method_card.content:
A tally chart is a quick way to count items as they occur. Each item is recorded with a vertical stroke; the fifth stroke is drawn diagonally across the previous four to form a bundle of five, making counting fast and accurate. Always group your tally marks into fives before reading totals.

A frequency table (or tabulation) organises data into categories with their corresponding frequencies. When data is numerical, it is grouped into class intervals — for example, “10 ≤ h < 20”. Each interval uses ≤ on the left and < on the right so that no value falls in two classes at once.

A pictogram uses a repeated symbol to represent data. The most important step is reading the key carefully: if one symbol represents 4 items, then half a symbol represents 2 items and a quarter symbol represents 1 item. The most common error at Foundation tier is ignoring the key and treating every symbol as worth 1.

When critiquing a diagram, look for these misrepresentation errors: a truncated axis (y-axis not starting at zero, which exaggerates differences), an incorrect scale (unequal gaps between tick marks), and distorted sizing (symbols at different sizes in a pictogram, or bar widths that vary). Any of these can mislead the reader about the size of differences in the data.

When choosing between formats: use a tally chart to collect live data; use a frequency table to present discrete or grouped data clearly; use a pictogram when the audience is non-specialist and the frequencies are whole multiples of the key value.
steps: Read the key on any pictogram before counting symbols
Multiply the number of complete symbols by the key value
For partial symbols, use the fraction shown (half symbol = half the key value)
Check a frequency table by summing all frequencies to get the total
Identify misrepresentation by checking whether the axis starts at zero and the scale is even
State why the misrepresentation is misleading, not just that it exists

exam_context.marks: 1–4 marks per question; pictogram reading is typically 1–2 marks, table completion up to 4 marks
exam_context.frequency: At least one tally/table/pictogram question appears on every paper; pictogram key errors are the single most common Foundation 1-mark drop

worked_examples.question: The pictogram below shows the number of books read by four students in a month. The key states: one symbol = 4 books. How many books did Priya read?

steps.label: Step 1 — Read the key
steps.content: Each complete symbol = 4 books. A half symbol = 2 books.

steps.label: Step 2 — Count Priya's row
steps.content: Priya has 3 complete symbols and 1 half symbol: \(3 \times 4 + 0.5 \times 4 = 12 + 2 = 14\) books.

worked_examples.question: The frequency table below shows the scores of 40 students on a quiz. Find the missing frequency for the 21–30 class.

A bar chart showing monthly rainfall has its y-axis starting at 20 mm rather than 0 mm. The bar for June reaches 30 mm and the bar for July reaches 60 mm. A student claims July had three times as much rainfall as June. Explain whether this is correct.

steps.label: Step 1 — Read the true values
steps.content: Both bars must be read from zero, not from the truncated axis origin. June = 30 mm; July = 60 mm.

steps.label: Step 2 — Calculate the true ratio
steps.content: \(\frac{60}{30} = 2\). July had twice as much rainfall, not three times.

steps.label: Step 3 — Explain the misrepresentation
steps.content: The truncated axis makes the bar for July appear three times the height of June’s bar on the chart, but the actual values show only a two-fold difference.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The student is wrong. The truncated axis exaggerates the visual difference. The true rainfall ratio is 2:1, not 3:1.

bronze.display: How many goals did Chelsea score?

misconceptions.message: Read the key first: 1 symbol = 6 goals. Chelsea has 2 full symbols (12) plus a half symbol (3). Total = 15. Do not count each symbol as 1 goal.

bronze.display: How many items were sold on Wednesday?

misconceptions.message: 1 symbol = 8 items. Wednesday: 1 full symbol (8) + half symbol (4) = 12. A half symbol represents half the key value.
Don't forget the half symbol: it represents 0.5 × 8 = 4 items, not 1 item or 0 items.
A bundle of 4 vertical strokes with a diagonal crossing stroke counts as 5. The Blue row shows one such bundle of 5, so frequency = 5.

What is the total frequency across all categories?

misconceptions.message: Add the frequency column: 1 + 4 + 6 = 11. The diagonal fifth stroke in a tally bundle is not an extra stroke.

bronze.display: How many students are in Year 7?

misconceptions.message: 1 symbol = 20 students. Year 7 has 3 complete symbols (60) and one quarter symbol (5). Total = 60 + 5 = 65. Re-check the picture: the partial symbol is a half, giving 3 × 20 + 0.5 × 20 = 70.

bronze.display: In a grouped frequency table for heights, which class interval correctly includes the value 150 cm?

misconceptions.message: Standard class intervals use ≤ on the left and < on the right. 150 satisfies 150 ≤ h < 160 (it is the left boundary of this class, not the right boundary of the one before).

misconceptions.message: Sum the known frequencies: 18 + 12 + 9 + 14 = 53. Missing = 60 − 53 = 7.

misconceptions.message: Tuesday: 4.5 × 50 = 225. Wednesday: 2 × 50 = 100. Difference = 225 − 100 = 125. Apply the key to both rows before subtracting.

A bar chart has its y-axis starting at 50 instead of 0. The bar for Group A reaches 80 and Group B reaches 100. A reporter claims Group B scored twice as many as Group A. Which response is correct?
options: Yes, because the bar for B is visually taller
No, because the true values are 80 and 100, a ratio of 4:5
Yes, because 100 is double 50
No, because both groups scored the same

misconceptions.message: True values are read from zero: 80 and 100. The ratio is 80:100 = 4:5, not 1:2. The truncated axis creates a visual illusion.

silver.display: A different month had 45 mm of rainfall. How many complete symbols should be drawn?

misconceptions.message: Number of symbols = 45 ÷ 5 = 9. The value must be an exact multiple of the key for complete symbols only.

silver.display: Which of these is NOT an example of graphical misrepresentation?
options: A bar chart with the y-axis starting at 30 rather than 0
A pictogram where each symbol represents a different number in different rows
A frequency table listing every class interval with equal width
A chart where the bars for larger categories are drawn physically wider

misconceptions.message: A frequency table with equal-width classes is correctly constructed. Options A, B and D all describe specific types of misrepresentation (truncated axis, inconsistent key, distorted sizing).

gold.display: How many more units did Product B sell than Product A?

misconceptions.message: Product A: 3.5 × 200 = 700. Product B: 2.25 × 400 = 900. B sold 200 more than A. Each product row has its own key — you cannot compare symbol counts directly.
Apply the correct key to each row before comparing. Product A uses the purple key (×200), Product B uses the amber key (×400).

Which statement correctly explains why a pictogram would NOT be appropriate for this data?
options: Pictograms can only show up to 4 categories
The frequencies are not all exact multiples of a simple key value, making symbols hard to draw accurately
Pictograms cannot show grouped numerical data
The total frequency is too large for a pictogram

misconceptions.message: Pictograms work best when frequencies are whole multiples of the key. Frequencies like 22 and 18 don’t divide neatly into simple symbols. The justification must refer to the data’s properties.

The original tally gave a total of 72 but the table shows 70. A bundle of 5 was likely miscounted as 3. In which class is the error most likely?
options: 0–5 min (frequency 14)
5–10 min (frequency 26)
10–15 min (frequency 19)
15–20 min (frequency 11)

misconceptions.message: The shortfall is 2 marks. If a bundle of 5 was read as 3, exactly 2 marks are missing. The largest class (26) has the most tally bundles and is most likely to contain this counting error.

gold.display: A pictogram showing the number of passengers on four train routes uses symbols of different sizes: routes with more passengers have bigger symbols. Each symbol still represents the same number. Does this pictogram contain a misrepresentation error?
options: No — as long as the key is the same, symbol size doesn't matter
Yes — varying symbol sizes create distorted sizing, misleading readers about relative frequencies
Yes — pictograms must always use exactly 10 symbols per row
No — larger symbols just make the chart easier to read

misconceptions.message: Distorted sizing is a recognised form of graphical misrepresentation. Even with a constant key, varying symbol sizes cause readers to perceive area differences rather than counting differences, exaggerating the apparent spread.

What fraction of matches saw the team score at least 2 goals? Give your answer in its simplest form.

misconceptions.message: At least 2 goals means 2, 3, or 4+: 9 + 6 + 3 = 18 matches. Total = 38. Fraction = 18/38 = 9/19.
Include the '4 or more goals' row — 'at least 2' includes all classes from 2 onwards.

A researcher needs to count vehicles passing a junction every 30 seconds over one hour, then present the results to a general audience. Which two formats would best serve these two purposes respectively?
options: Tally chart to record; frequency table to present
Pictogram to record; tally chart to present
Tally chart to record; pictogram to present
Frequency table to record; pictogram to present

misconceptions.message: A tally chart is best for recording live data quickly. A pictogram is best for a general audience who can interpret symbols more easily than raw numbers. A frequency table is better for analysis than audience presentation in this context.
